5.12.s.en: 7. "His hands are rings of gold set with beryl" [14].

5.12.0.en: The "ring" or "circle" signifies eternity, because it has no starting point and no end point. His hands are eternal, satisfying soul and body together forever. As for their being of gold, this is a reference to their heavenly character... For He takes hold of His bride and puts her hand in His heavenly hand to pour out His work in her, so that she bears His heavenly power and potentialities, to cross with Him to heaven.

5.12.1.en: As for the beryl, it appears repeatedly in the Old Testament (Ezek 1:16; Dan 10:6), to signify the power of founding... for "the works of his hands are verity and judgment," and both hands establish His bride on firm faith and truth.

5.13.s.en: 8. "His belly is white ivory overlaid with blue sapphire" [14].

5.13.0.en: The belly, or the bowels, signifies God's deep feelings, full of love and tenderness, as in Jeremiah: "my bowels are troubled for him; I will surely have mercy upon him, saith the LORD" (Jer 31:20). As for this tenderness being like white ivory, it is because ivory comes as the fruit of suffering, for it is taken from the elephant through its sufferings unto death. And as for His bowels being overlaid with blue sapphire, a heavenly color, it is to declare that His love is not earthly and temporary but heavenly and eternal.

5.14.s.en: 9. "His legs are pillars of marble set upon sockets of fine gold (gold)" [15].

5.14.0.en: The legs signify the ability to walk steadily, and the gold or fine gold signifies the heavenly nature, as though whoever is united with the Bridegroom is able to walk with Him in continual movement toward heaven, trampling beneath his feet all the powers of the devil, shattering death and conquering sin.

5.14.1.en: St. Ambrose has a beautiful comment on this phrase, for he says: [His legs are pillars of marble set upon sockets of gold, because Christ walks in souls, and makes for Himself ways in the minds of His saints, so that it is in them as though they were two bases of gold and foundations of precious stones, upon which are imprinted the footprints of the heavenly Word of God].

5.15.s.en: 10. "His countenance is like Lebanon, a youth like the cedar" [15].

5.15.0.en: Lebanon is a beautiful tourist region to which some newlyweds resort to begin their married life in a beautiful atmosphere; so too the face of the Lord Jesus, with the cheerfulness and tenderness it bears, gladdens the soul that wants to live the spiritual married life with the divine Word. The psalmist described the Messiah, saying: "Thou art fairer than the children of men," and in the report which Pontius Pilate wrote to Herod about the Lord Christ it came: "you long to look upon Him."

5.15.1.en: As for the secret of His beauty, it lies in His being "a youth like the cedar," known for its towering height together with its uprightness and its sweet scent... Thus the Lord Christ appears to the soul as the youth who never grows old.

5.15.2.en: And the wonder is that the Lord in His condescension took on our humanity, sharing with us all the stages of growth except old age: He became an embryo among embryos, and a child among children, a boy and a youth and then a man, but He ascended before old age, for it was not fitting for Him to grow old, lest His Church bear the spirit of weakness and spiritual old age. For it came in the divine inspiration: "thy youth is renewed like the eagle's" (Ps 103:5). And it came in the rite of the Church concerning the Church and the Virgin Mary, as the ideal member of the Church: "the vine that does not grow old"...

5.15.3.en: The Christian never knows old age at all, but grows younger with the days, for though his outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day (2 Cor 4:16), and as the Apostle Paul says: "ye have put on the new man, which is renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him" (Col 3:10)... Truly, the body weakens and may grow old, but the spirit remains active and strong (Mt 26:41; Mk 14:38).

5.16.s.en: This is my beloved, and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem" [16].

5.16.0.en: The psalmist says: "How sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth" (Ps 119:103). So the believer finds in the words of the Lord a special sweetness and delight, because these words are spirit and life. He who eats of them returns to the Lord hungry for Him, and he who drinks of Him thirsts for Him all the more...

5.16.1.en: When man listens to the words of the Lord his heart is drawn with greater longing to know these divine mysteries, and he remains all his life sitting at the feet of the Lord, not wanting to leave Him, saying with the psalmist: "I have seen an end of all perfection: but thy commandment is exceeding broad" (Ps 119).

5.16.2.en: The secret of the sweetness of His words is that they carry power and authority, for He does not give mere commandments or advice and guidance or warnings, but gives with the word the power to carry it out, so that the commandment lifts man to enter into the knowledge of the mysteries of heaven, and the soul goes from glory to glory, continually bearing the secret of a new power that never ends.

5.16.3.en: Finally, since the bride feels the inability of language to describe her Bridegroom, she says: "He is altogether lovely." This is her Beloved, the Friend whom she seeks and strives after... He satisfies her; in Him she finds all her love, and to Him is all her longing!

6.0.0.en: When the soul bears witness to her Bridegroom, unbelievers begin to ask:

6.0.1.en: "Whither is thy beloved gone, O thou fairest among women?

6.0.2.en: Whither is thy beloved turned aside? that we may seek him with thee" [1].

6.0.3.en: Since the soul's testimony about the Bridegroom bore the reflections of His glory on her life and conduct, they called her "the fairest among women." Even the sight of her in her spiritual beauty generated in them a special attraction, not that they might cling to her in herself, but to search for her Bridegroom, who is the secret of her beauty!

6.0.4.en: They came into intense longing for Him together with perplexity, and they asked: "Where has your Beloved gone? Where did He turn? Where has He hidden? We want to know Him with you, and to go in to Him, not without you." The unbelievers realized that they cannot get to know this Bridegroom outside the Church, but with her and through her, that He is the Bridegroom of the Church; therefore in order to go in to Him it is fitting for them to accept membership in the Church... Thus He becomes a head for them. For without the Church the world does not know Christ, and outside Christ there is no Church.

6.1.0.en: As for the Church's answer, it is:

6.1.1.en: "My beloved is gone down into his garden, to the beds of spices, to feed in the gardens, and to gather lilies.

6.1.2.en: I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine: the Shepherd among the lilies" [2-3].

6.1.3.en: It is not strange that this book contains continual assurances of the presence of the Bridegroom within the Church, and His presence within the soul that He acquired with His blood. For He enters the barren stony heart and makes of it a garden for Himself (Song 4:12, 16; 5:1), indeed inner gardens in which He feeds, and there He gathers the lilies that bear the features of the Bridegroom Himself, who was also called the lily (Song 2:1).

6.1.4.en: It is as though the bride here warns against wasting time searching for the Bridegroom outside, for in His humility He came down to His Church and entered the hearts of His people. Therefore the Apostle says: "Say not in thine heart, Who shall ascend into heaven? (that is, to bring Christ down)... The word is nigh thee, even in thy mouth, and in thy heart" (Rom 10:7-8).

6.1.5.en: Furthermore, in the bride's answer there is a clarification, for those outside, of the secret of the relationship between the soul and God: if God has entered into His garden to gather lilies, He does not do so as one who exploits His creation or as a lover of domination and taking, but He entered in response to a call of love issued to Him from her, for she says to Him, "I am my beloved's." As though she says: All that is mine is my Beloved's, let Him enter my heart and receive the whole heart and all the inner energies and feelings, for what I possess is His. And this call is nothing but a response to the work of love which He showed her, since "my beloved is mine." He gave me His life... and here I return His love with love! I love Him with the fullness of my choice, since He loved me with the fullness of His freedom.

6.1.6.en: As for her saying "gone down," it means her declaration of the truth of the situation, that the Bridegroom's coming down to her heart is not out of need on His part nor for humiliation, but is a condescension from Him to accept my invitation to come down into my life, that He may raise me up with Him to His heavens, taking me wholly as He gave me Himself.

6.1.7.en: He has come down into my heart... so what shall I ask? It is not fitting for me to ask of Him anything but to take Him Himself, and nothing but this request suffices me or satisfies my soul. For no earthly reward nor gifts or presents can quench my thirst, but I ask for Him... "my beloved is mine."

6.2.s.en: The Bridegroom's conversation with His bride in the garden:

6.2.0.en: 1. "Thou art beautiful, O my love, as Tirzah, comely as Jerusalem, terrible as an army with banners (in order)" [4].

6.2.1.en: When the bride enters into a relationship of union with her Bridegroom, each speaks intimately to the other. And now, since the bride has declared to the unbelievers and testified that He is within her in His garden, and asks them not to search for Him outside, the Bridegroom praises her, using some of the earlier expressions (Song 4) while revealing a deeper beauty, delighted by her entering into a deeper union with Him.

6.2.2.en: Here He sees her "beautiful as Tirzah." The word "Tirzah" in Hebrew means "delight or joy." And Tirzah is the youngest of the five daughters of Zelophehad the son of Hepher (Num 26:33); these daughters, whose father had died and who had no brother, stood before Moses and Eleazar the priest and before the princes and all the congregation by the door of the tabernacle of the congregation and asked to inherit their father's property with their father's brothers, and the Lord gave them this right and it became a statute of judgment (Num 27:1-11), and they also received their portion at the division of the land by Joshua the son of Nun (Josh 17:3-6). Perhaps in the Song of Songs the bride is likened to Tirzah as the youngest of the daughters who claimed their right before Moses the prophet and Joshua, and the command was issued from the Lord that they receive an inheritance and portion. This is the beauty of the soul united with Christ Jesus, that she in boldness without fear asks for her inheritance and portion, that is, her right to live as a living member in the holy congregation. And what is this inheritance or this portion that belongs to the believer but the Lord Himself, whom the soul receives within her as the secret of her glory and wealth.

6.2.3.en: And perhaps by "Tirzah" is meant the exceedingly beautiful city that originally belonged to the Canaanites, which Joshua the son of Nun took (Josh 12:24) and gave to the tribes of the children of Israel. It was the capital of the kingdom of Israel (the ten tribes) for about fifty years (1 Kgs 14:17; 15:21, 31; 16:6, 23) until Omri built Samaria. The secret of its beauty was that it had formerly been Gentile and idolatrous, but when the true Joshua reigned over it, it became the possession of the Lord.

6.2.4.en: And the Lord also sees her "comely as Jerusalem"; the secret of her comeliness is that she is like Jerusalem, the city of the King. That is, the Church has come to represent the heavenly sanctuaries in which God dwells, and the capital of the sphere of His kingdom, in which everything is beautiful and radiant.

6.2.5.en: Her beauty like Tirzah's or her comeliness like Jerusalem's has been mingled with strength, for she is "terrible as an army with banners (in order)," terrible before the enemies, because the victorious Lord in her midst protects her; she is like a heavenly army bearing the banners (flags) of victory and triumph, knowing neither defeat nor despair but the spirit of victory and strength. And according to the Greek translation, she is like an army well ordered, since its Commander is the Lord Himself.

6.3.0.en: In other words, the Christian bears strength together with beauty, being beautiful in his meekness and gentleness as well as strong in his courage and firmness. He is beautiful in his inner calm and mighty in his striving against sin unto blood. And the secret of his strength and victory is the "tears" which he pours out with a broken heart before God, which captivate the divine love, as the Lord says to him:

6.3.1.en: "Turn away thine eyes from me, for they have overcome me" [5].

6.3.2.en: The mercies of God were overcome by the tears of the sinful woman and the sighs of the right-hand thief. For God cannot bear to see man's tears and contrition, and perhaps the greatest example of this is Ahab the wicked king, who killed and also inherited (1 Kgs 21:19), of whom Scripture testified: "But there was none like unto Ahab, which did sell himself to work wickedness in the sight of the LORD, whom Jezebel his wife stirred up. And he did very abominably in following idols..." (1 Kgs 21:25-26); when he heard the word of the Lord against him by the mouth of Elijah the prophet he rent his clothes and put sackcloth upon his flesh and lay in sackcloth and went softly; the Lord could not bear this sight but said to Elijah the prophet: "Seest thou how Ahab humbleth himself before me? because he humbleth himself before me, I will not bring the evil in his days" (1 Kgs 21:29).

6.4.0.en: 2. "Thy hair is as a flock of goats lying down in Gilead. Thy teeth are as a flock of sheep which come up from the washing, whereof every one beareth twins, and there is not one barren among them, (thy lips are like a thread of scarlet, thy speech is sweet), thy cheek is like a piece of a pomegranate (seen) within thy veil" [5-7].

6.4.1.en: He had already praised her with the same attributes in chapter four (1-3), which we have already treated in some detail. As for the secret of His repeating the same expressions, it is to confirm an important truth, that God's love for man remains unchanging. For in spite of the lukewarmness man suffered - as came in chapter five - yet when she returned to Him with the tears of repentance she found Him praising her with the same expressions with which He had praised her before, and His look toward her had not changed, but His love for her increases. Perhaps this reminds us of God's dealings with the Apostle Peter, to whom, even after his denial, the Lord affirmed three times his acceptance in the apostolic work, saying to him: "Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me?... Feed my sheep!" As though God's love does not change, but it depends on our love, which changes... His divine arms are still open with love.

6.5.0.en: 3. "There are threescore queens, and fourscore concubines, and virgins without number. One is my dove, my perfect one;

6.5.1.en: she is the only one of her mother, she is the choice one (the chosen) of her that bare her.

6.5.2.en: The daughters saw her, and blessed her; the queens and the concubines, and they praised her" [8-9].

6.5.3.en: He praises her through the language of numbers... So what does He mean by the sixty queens? And the eighty concubines? And the virgins without number? And His one perfect dove?!

6.5.4.en: First: perhaps He compared her with the heavenly creation that loves Him, and saw the heavenly ones as many orders, whom He likened to the sixty queens and the eighty concubines and the virgins without number... These are of varying degrees as to stature, but His Church, which the Bridegroom acquired with His blood and sanctified by His Holy Spirit, has become the one bride, the perfect dove... This is the secret of her beauty and perfection and strength: she has become the one Body of the Lord, though she comprises many members, for He "gathers together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad" (Jn 11:52), gathered together in Him (Eph 1:10).

6.5.5.en: As for the secret of her unity, it does not consist merely in the members' gathering together in one place, or their uniting in one language or one culture... but consists in the following divine factors:

6.5.6.en: a. She is His dove... If there is one Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of the Father and the Son together, then He gave His Church this divine Spirit to set believers in motion as one dove, receiving the life of fellowship with God. This is the work of the Holy Spirit: He grants believers fellowship with God and with one another, for since by Him we are reconciled with the Father in the merits of the blood of the Son, we receive in Baptism the Spirit of adoption by which we cry "Abba, Father" (Rom 8:15). Through this reconciliation we see ourselves members one of another.

6.5.7.en: We quote here some words of the Fathers in this matter:

6.5.8.en: * By the Holy Spirit, who gathers the people of God into one, the evil spirit, divided against itself, is driven out.

6.5.9.en: * It belongs to the Holy Spirit to give the fellowship by which we have become one body of the one only Son of God, for it is written: "If there be therefore any consolation in Christ, if any comfort of love, if any fellowship of the Spirit" (Phil 2:1).

6.5.10.en: St. Augustine * When the Most High came down and confused the tongues, He divided the nations.

6.5.11.en: But when He distributed the tongues of fire (the Holy Spirit) He called all to unity; therefore with one accord we glorify the all-holy Spirit.

6.6.s.en: The hymn Kontakon for the feast of Pentecost

6.6.1.en: b. She is His perfect one: since the Church puts on the perfect Lord Christ, she becomes perfect through Him, and her unity is based on entering into the "new perfect life" that we have in Christ Jesus. In this new life we are not subject to the law of schism or the spirit of enmity, but rather to the spirit of love, which grants inner unity. Thus our unity comes through our sanctification by union with the Holy One, so that we imitate the unity of the Holy Trinity... This is what appears clearly in the Lord's farewell prayer, on the night of His passion, when He says:

6.6.2.en: "Holy Father, keep through thine own name those whom thou hast given me, that they may be one, as we are.

6.6.3.en: That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee,

6.6.4.en: that they also may be one...

6.6.5.en: I in them, and thou in me, that they may be made perfect in one" (Jn 17).

6.6.6.en: Regarding this the martyr St. Cyprian says: [This is what He longed for us: that we live in the same pattern of unity that exists between the Father and the Son in their being one].

6.6.7.en: And St. Cyril of Alexandria says: [He desires for us a union with one another after the same pattern as the unity of the Holy Trinity... this unity, which is the most perfect union, must be reflected in the unity of the believers].

6.6.8.en: c. The only one of her mother and the chosen of her that bare her: Who is this mother or this bearer who looks upon the Church as her only one and chosen one?! It is the heavenly Jerusalem, whose work is nothing but waiting for this one bride whom the Lord Jesus betrothed, to remain a partner in glory forever. As though the secret of unity springs from the believers' entering into eternity... or their departure from the sphere of time. For if our temporal life breeds the spirit of schism and jealousy, then our enjoyment of the pledge of the heavenly things grants us love toward all humanity and longing on an eternal level. For the law of heaven is peace and unity, and its language is love.

6.6.9.en: The Bridegroom says: "The daughters saw her, and blessed her; the queens and the concubines, and they praised her," that is, the heavenly ones bless her, for they see that she has submitted to their law and spoken their language, and has become one of them and not a stranger to them.

6.6.10.en: Second: the language of the symbolic numbers can be understood as declarations about the secret of the Church's beauty, perfection, and strength:

6.6.11.en: a. Sixty queens: the Church is likened to sixty queens, because if the number 12 represents the kingdom of God on earth, as we saw before, since the Holy Trinity reigns over the four quarters of the world (3 x 4), then since God reigns over the five senses of believers (12 x 5), the number sixty is a symbol of God's kingship over the life of believers, or over the life of the Church extended to all the quarters of the world. Thus the Church becomes sixty queens... the King of kings reigns in us, so our life is not in slavery but rises to bear royal glory.

6.6.12.en: b. Eighty concubines: in the first number the Church appeared as a queen through God's reign over her senses, but here the Church appears as a concubine, that is, living a hidden spiritual life with the Bridegroom. As for the number eighty, it signifies the Church's being marked with the eschatological nature while still on earth. For the number 10 signifies our temporal life, therefore the Ten Commandments came in the Old Testament as a divine law that we practice on earth, but the number 8 (10 x 8) signifies the other life, as we saw before, because it exceeds the number 7, which signifies the week of our life. Therefore circumcision came on the eighth day, and the Lord rose on the first day of the new week, or the eighth of the previous week, and eight souls were saved in Noah's ark... all of these signify the new upper or heavenly life. So the Church, while living on earth (10), lives the new heavenly life (8).

6.6.13.en: c. Virgins without number: this unlimited number signifies the virginity of the whole life for the Lord, so the believer offers a virgin heart that accepts no bridegroom other than the Lord, and a virgin mind that thinks only of the things of the Lord, and virgin feelings... therefore the kingdom of God was likened to virgins who went out to meet the bridegroom.

6.6.14.en: d. The one: the oneness of the Church is a principal feature in the life of the Church, for the believer declares "We believe in one holy catholic apostolic Church," and we have already seen the secret of this oneness...

6.6.15.en: Her sonship to the one God the Father by her union with Christ through the Holy Spirit in Baptism.

6.6.16.en: St. Irenaeus sees that the secret of this unity is also "the unity of faith," for he says: [The true Church, which is truly ancient, is one Church... The early catholic Church alone works in the unity of the faith].

6.6.17.en: And in Father Rufinus' discourse on the Apostles' Creed he mentioned this phrase (Song 6:9), explaining that the secret of this unity is the one faith, for he says: [Whoever receives this faith in the Church, let him not go outside to vain counsel, nor take part with workers of iniquity].

6.7.0.en: And we can understand "My dove, my perfect one, is but one" to be St. Mary the Virgin, for many received honor, but she surpassed them all, and it came in the Sunday Theotokia:

6.7.1.en: "Hail to you, O Mary, the beautiful dove, who bore for us God the Word"

6.7.2.en: And what is mentioned in the Song afterward applies to her: "Who is she that looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, pure as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners (in order)?" [10]. She is radiant as the morning, for from her became incarnate the Sun of Righteousness, who shone on us who sat in darkness for a time. And she is fair as the moon, deriving her beauty from the light of her Son. Pure or chosen as the sun, for the Holy Spirit came upon her, who purified her and prepared her for the divine Incarnation. Terrible as an army in order, for she bears within her the Lord of hosts, the Commander of the battle against sin and the kingdom of the devil.

6.7.3.en: We can also understand the text in another way, for every soul that meets with God and bears His Holy Spirit within her through the Church and puts on Christ Jesus, the Lord calls her by her name, and shines in her with His light, so she becomes radiant without darkness, fair as the moon, chosen and beautiful by His blood, terrible and victorious by His Cross.

6.8.0.en: "I went down into the garden of nuts to see the greens of the valley, and to see whether the vine flourished,

6.8.2.en: There will I give thee my breasts. I did not perceive until my soul had made me like the chariots of Amminadab (a noble people).

6.8.3.en: Return, return, O Shulamite; return, return, that we may look upon thee.

6.8.4.en: What will ye see in the Shulamite?

6.8.5.en: Like the ordering of ranks in a camp (like the dance of two ranks)" [11-13].

6.8.6.en: If the Lord has praised His bride thus, the bride, before this great love, did not stand to listen to the praise but went down to her inner valley to work, went down to the garden of nuts and gave attention to the vine and the pomegranate tree.

6.8.7.en: What does the garden of nuts mean? The scholar Origen answers: [The bride went down to the garden of nuts to discover that the nut had put forth its fruit in a priestly way], for the rod of Aaron the high priest budded and bore the fruit of nuts (Num 17:8).

6.8.8.en: And the nut in truth represents the word of God, which occupies the heart of the priest continually, offering it as a rich table for his people to eat and be satisfied and bear much fruit. When the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah the son of Hilkiah the priest, he was asked: "What seest thou, Jeremiah?" And he said: "I see a rod of an almond tree," then the Lord said to him: "Thou hast well seen: for I am watching over my word to perform it" (Jer 1:11-12).

6.8.9.en: And the scholar Origen explains the use of the "nut" as a symbol of the word of God by saying that the nut has a bitter outer covering, the husk, which dries and falls off, then the thick inner covering, which is broken so that man may eat the sweet inner fruit. Thus the scholar sees that the word of God has the bitter literal interpretation which the Jews used, then the moral or behavioral interpretation, which is like the thick shell, where it drives man to a life of faithfulness (the breaking), striving unto blood, to enter into the sweet spiritual meaning, which is granted as food for the spiritual, by which they live not only in this world but also in the next world.

6.8.10.en: Therefore behold, the soul has gone down into her inner depths as into the garden of the word of God working in her; there she sees the fruits of the valley. There in the heart she perceives the spiritual meanings of the word that satisfy her, as though she says to the Bridegroom: If You have praised me thus, I have no merit, but it is the fruit of Your divine word planted within me by Your divine hand.

6.8.11.en: And the wonder is that the Lord's praise of the faithful soul does not drive her to pride but pricks her to work, so she goes down to see the Lord's vineyard that is within her and the trees which His right hand planted: has the vine flowered?! Have the pomegranates blossomed?!

6.8.12.en: When she enters the garden of the Lord within her and touches His work in her, she rejoices in the fruit even though it is still at the beginning, and speaks intimately with her Bridegroom: "There will I give thee my breasts"... as though she says to Him: I return Your love with love. You offered me Your breasts, which are the Old Testament and the New Testament, and behold Your word has borne fruit within me, so I return to You what is Yours: I give You my breasts, that is, I offer You the same two Testaments. For Your book has become my book! But how does she offer Him these two breasts? When she bears practical witness to the word of God before others and offers the word to her brethren, she has offered it to the Bridegroom Himself... as He says: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me" (Mt 25:40).

6.8.13.en: Though she sees in the vine only a flower and in the pomegranate also its "blossom," she perceived that God had made her soul like the chariots of Amminadab or the chariots of a noble people. For the word "Amminadab" means "my people are noble." By the power of the word she has become the honored people of God, fighting and striving to the end against sin.

6.8.14.en: Her view of herself as the chariots of Amminadab carried other meanings also, among them: 1. Amminadab the father of Nahshon (Ruth 4:19; Ex 6:23) of the tribe of Judah, from whose seed came the Lord Christ; so the secret of her honor is her belonging to the King Christ, the true Commander of the chariots, by whom we conquer completely. 2. Another Amminadab of the sons of Uzziel, a Levite, one of the chiefs whom King David chose to carry the ark of the covenant (1 Chr 15:3, 10)... as though the soul has been granted in the New Testament to carry Christ Himself within her... this is the secret of her fruitfulness and sanctification. 3. Amminadab the son of Kohath, also of the Levites (1 Chr 6:24)... whom David the prophet appointed with others to sing or praise in the house of the Lord after the ark came to rest (1 Chr 6:31)... as though this is the work of the soul united with Christ Jesus her Bridegroom: "continual praise."

6.8.15.en: So the Church, or the soul as a member of the Church, finds herself in a state of striving and warfare under the leadership of the Bridegroom, sanctified by Him, praising Him and thanking Him!

6.8.16.en: In this atmosphere full of striving with joy and praise the Bridegroom calls His bride, saying:

6.9.0.en: Return, return, that we may look upon thee." [13].

6.9.1.en: He called her "Shulamite," which is the feminine of "Shalem or Salem or Solomon," as though the Lord Christ, who is the true Solomon, calls her by His own title. She bore His person within her, and His traits in her conduct, and His name was called upon her.

6.9.2.en: He looks at her while she is in a state of war and calls her "Shulamite," that is, the bearer of peace! And the secret of her peace is her continual return to Him... and that the Holy Trinity looks at her and cares for her and does not forget her... "Return, return, that we may look upon thee."

6.9.3.en: He returns and looks at those around Him, saying:

6.9.4.en: What will ye see in the Shulamite?!

6.9.5.en: Like the ordering of ranks in a camp (like the dance of two ranks)" [13].

6.9.6.en: The Lord Christ takes pride in His Church, or in the soul that is a member of His Church, for He sees her, bearing peace within her, as having become like ordered ranks of soldiers for spiritual warfare!

6.9.7.en: And according to the Hebrew text He sees her as "the dance of two ranks"; the word "two ranks" means "two armies." As though the Lord declares that His Church has borne the dances of the two armies as a sign of victory and triumph. This reminds us of the dances of joy performed by Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, with the rest of the women, as they praised the Lord who delivered them from Pharaoh and his army (Ex 15:20). And also when David the prophet killed Goliath the giant, the women came out of all the cities singing and dancing (1 Sam 18:6).
